title: Designing Under Ambiguity
summary: Making progress when the interviewer deliberately withholds requirements or context, by stating and testing assumptions instead of stalling on a fourth question.

slides.markdown:
Some interviews go beyond ordinary ambiguity — the interviewer deliberately withholds a number or a requirement, even after you ask, to see how you handle incomplete information. This isn't the interviewer being unhelpful; it's a specific skill under test.

The move that works is stating a reasonable assumption out loud and proceeding, then checking back in as more context appears — not repeatedly re-asking the same question, and not freezing until it's answered for you.

slides.sectionTitle: Why interviewers withhold information on purpose
slides.markdown:
In real engineering work, you rarely get a complete spec before you start — a product manager doesn't know the exact scale, a stakeholder hasn't decided a policy, a dependency's behavior under failure is genuinely unknown until it's tested. Interviewers who withhold a number are simulating that condition specifically, not being cagey for its own sake.

A candidate who can only make progress with a fully specified problem is signaling that they'd stall on real ambiguous work too. A candidate who states "I'll assume X, and I'll flag if that turns out to matter" and keeps moving is demonstrating exactly the skill that ambiguity-testing is checking for.

Recognizing this reframes withheld information from an obstacle into the actual test.

slides.sectionTitle: Stating an assumption out loud instead of asking a fourth clarifying question
slides.markdown:
If you've asked about scale two or three times in different phrasings and gotten "whatever you think is reasonable" each time, asking a fourth way is unlikely to produce a number — it's more likely to read as stalling. The better move is stating your own number and moving forward with it visibly.

"I'll assume roughly a million daily active users with a 10:1 read-to-write ratio, since that's typical for this kind of app — I'll flag anywhere this assumption matters a lot" does three things at once: it unblocks you, it shows your reasoning for the number chosen, and it invites a correction if the real number is wildly different.

This differs from silently guessing, which hides the assumption, and from repeatedly asking, which burns time without new information.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the assumption → decision → checkpoint loop under ambiguity
slides.markdown:
![Loop: state an assumption, make a decision on it, checkpoint out loud, repeat for the next unknown](assets/ambiguity-loop.svg)

Designing under ambiguity isn't one big guess at the start — it's this loop repeated in miniature every time a new unknown appears, each one small enough that being wrong costs little.

The checkpoint step matters as much as the assumption itself: it's what turns a silent guess into a collaborative, correctable one.

assets.alt: Loop: state an assumption, make a decision on it, checkpoint out loud, repeat for the next unknown

slides.sectionTitle: Making a defensible call with incomplete information
slides.markdown:
A defensible assumption isn't the same as an arbitrary one — it should come from a stated reason, even a rough one: industry norms for a similar system, the most conservative case, or whichever assumption is cheapest to change later if it's wrong.

For example, if you don't know whether a feed needs to support real-time updates, assuming "not real-time" first is defensible because it's the cheaper design to extend toward real-time later, rather than the reverse — over-building for real-time and finding out it was never needed.

Saying the reasoning behind the assumption, not just the assumption itself, is what makes it a defensible engineering call rather than a coin flip that happened to be stated out loud.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: guessing silently vs narrating your reasoning under uncertainty
slides.markdown:
Both approaches let you keep moving forward under an unanswered question — they differ entirely in what the interviewer can see.

| | Silent guessing | Narrating your reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| What's visible | Only the resulting design | The assumption, the reason for it, and the design |
| Correction cost if wrong | High — the interviewer may not notice until much later | Low — the interviewer can redirect immediately |
| Reads as | Hoping it doesn't come up | Comfortable operating under real uncertainty |
| Interviewer's typical response | None, until a later contradiction surfaces | Often confirms or adjusts the assumption right away |

**How to decide:** always narrate the assumption, even briefly — the cost of saying it is a sentence; the cost of a silent wrong guess is a design that quietly stops matching the problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: freezing up when the interviewer won't just answer the question
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I can't design this properly until I know the real number, so I should keep asking until they tell me."

**Why it's wrong:** treating an unanswered question as a blocker rather than a deliberate condition of the exercise stalls the entire interview — and "I need more information to proceed" repeated several times reads as an inability to operate under realistic uncertainty, which is the opposite of what the interviewer is trying to see.

**Correct model:** after one or two honest attempts to get a number, assume one, state it and the reasoning behind it, and keep moving — treating the assumption as provisional and easy to revise the moment better information appears, rather than as a permanent gap you're stuck behind.

slides.sectionTitle: A default assumption stack you can reach for under pressure
slides.subTitle: Estimation
slides.markdown:
Rather than deriving every assumption from scratch under time pressure, keep a small default stack you reach for and adjust, then state it out loud rather than silently baking it in.

A workable default bundle for most consumer-scale systems: **read:write ratio** around 10:1 to 100:1 unless the domain says otherwise (chat and messaging skew closer to 1:1); **availability over strict consistency** for anything that isn't money or inventory; **eventual consistency acceptable** within a few seconds for counters, view counts, and feeds; **peak traffic** at roughly 3-5x average, not 100x, unless the product is explicitly viral/spiky (ticket drops, flash sales).

The takeaway: having defaults ready means ambiguity costs you a sentence ("I'll assume X unless you tell me otherwise") instead of a stall.

slides.sectionTitle: Staff-level nuance: revisiting a design when an assumption breaks
slides.markdown:
A design built on a stated assumption isn't fixed once you state it — if the interviewer later reveals something that contradicts it, the strongest move is to visibly revisit the design, not quietly keep going as if nothing changed.

Concrete example: you assumed eventual consistency was fine for a "like count," built a design around an async counter service, and the interviewer then says "actually, likes need to reflect instantly for the creator's own dashboard." The staff-level response names the impact directly: "That changes things — the creator's own view now needs a synchronous read path, everyone else's can stay eventually consistent," then sketches the one component that needs to change rather than the whole diagram.

**Testing:** whether you treat new information as a signal to update the design, the way a real requirements change would, instead of defending the original assumption.
